title: Bordeaux
description: Two rivers, an estuary and the Atlantic: the region that defined the red blend and the château.
L: Explain its history as a trading port

Bordeaux lies in south-west France, around the Garonne and Dordogne rivers, which meet to form the Gironde estuary before reaching the Atlantic. It has about 110,000 hectares of vines, one of the largest fine wine regions in the world. Soils vary: gravel on the Left Bank, clay and limestone on the Right.

The climate is maritime: mild winters, warm summers and rain throughout the year. The Atlantic and the Gulf Stream moderate temperatures; the Landes pine forest shelters vineyards from ocean winds. Rain at flowering or harvest can hurt a vintage, which is why vintage quality varies so much, and why blending several grapes spreads the risk.
Why do Bordeaux vintages vary so much?
Its maritime climate brings rain at key moments
Rain at flowering or harvest can change a year's quality.

Bordeaux's wealth came from trade. From 1152 to 1453, when Aquitaine belonged to the English crown, its light red wine, called claret, flowed to England. Later, Dutch merchants drained the Médoc's marshes in the 17th century, creating the great Left Bank estates. Négociants still sell most of Bordeaux's wine through the Place de Bordeaux.
Claret, the English and the Dutch
Bordeaux's soils are gravel, clay and limestone, not volcanic.
Bordeaux sits on the Garonne, Dordogne and Gironde
Its maritime climate makes vintages vary
Trade with England and the Dutch shaped its history
Name Bordeaux's red and white grapes

Bordeaux's reds blend Merlot, the most planted grape, about 60% of red vines, Cabernet Sauvignon, Cabernet Franc, and small amounts of Petit Verdot, Malbec and Carmenère. Since 2021, a few heat-tolerant grapes like Touriga Nacional can be used in small amounts, under trial rules.

Each grape ripens at a different time and suits different soils. Merlot ripens early and likes cool clay; Cabernet Sauvignon ripens late and needs warm gravel; Cabernet Franc adds perfume. In a difficult year, blending lets the winemaker lean on whichever grape did best. Whites blend Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon, sometimes Muscadelle.
Match each grape to its role.
Each grape fills a gap in the blend.
Bordeaux labels rarely name grapes. The appellation tells you: Left Bank wines lean on Cabernet Sauvignon, Right Bank wines on Merlot.
Cabernet Sauvignon is Bordeaux's most planted red grape.
Not true. Merlot is the most planted, about 60% of red vines.
Merlot, Cabernet Sauvignon and Cabernet Franc lead the reds
Blending spreads risk and balances flavour
Whites blend Sauvignon Blanc and Sémillon
Compare the Left and Right Banks
Explain how soil drives the difference

The Left Bank, west of the Garonne and Gironde, includes the Médoc and Graves. Deep gravel soils drain well and store heat, favouring Cabernet Sauvignon. The Haut-Médoc's famous communes are Saint-Estèphe, Pauillac, Saint-Julien and Margaux. Graves and Pessac-Léognan, further south, make both reds and whites.
Médoc and Graves: Cabernet on gravel

The Right Bank, north of the Dordogne, includes Saint-Émilion, Pomerol and their satellites, Fronsac and the Côtes. Cooler clay and limestone suit Merlot and Cabernet Franc. Estates are smaller and often family-run. Between the rivers, Entre-Deux-Mers makes mostly dry whites.
Saint-Émilion and Pomerol: Merlot on clay
Match each appellation to its bank.

Left Bank wines are often more structured, with blackcurrant, cedar and firm tannins, built for long ageing. Right Bank wines are often rounder, plummier and softer young. Saint-Émilion's limestone plateau gives freshness; Pomerol's clay gives richness. These are tendencies, not rules.
Why does Cabernet Sauvignon dominate on the Left Bank?
Gravel soils drain and store heat, helping it ripen
Gravel's warmth helps a late-ripening grape.
The Left Bank's gravel favours Cabernet Sauvignon
The Right Bank's clay and limestone favour Merlot
Left Bank wines are more structured; Right Bank rounder

For the 1855 Exposition Universelle in Paris, Napoleon III asked Bordeaux's brokers to rank the region's wines. They used prices. The red list ranked 61 châteaux, all from the Médoc except Haut-Brion in Graves, into five growths, or crus. Sauternes and Barsac were ranked separately, with Yquem on top.

The 1855 classification has changed only twice: Cantemerle was added soon after in 1856, and in 1973 Mouton Rothschild was promoted from Second to First Growth. The five First Growths are Lafite Rothschild, Latour, Margaux, Haut-Brion and Mouton Rothschild. Some Fifth Growths now sell for more than some Seconds.
Which château was promoted to First Growth in 1973?
Baron Philippe de Rothschild campaigned for decades for the promotion.

Graves has its own classification, from 1953 and 1959. Saint-Émilion's classification, from 1955, is revised about every ten years and has been controversial. Pomerol has no official classification. The Crus Bourgeois of the Médoc, re-established in 2020, rank hundreds of other estates.
Pétrus, in Pomerol, was never classified; Pomerol has no classification.
The 1855 classification ranked Médoc reds and Sauternes by price
It has changed only twice, in 1856 and 1973
Graves, Saint-Émilion and the Crus Bourgeois have their own rankings
Explain how noble rot forms in Sauternes

Sauternes and Barsac lie in southern Graves, where the cold Ciron river flows into the warmer Garonne. On autumn mornings, the difference in temperature creates mist, ideal for noble rot, Botrytis cinerea. Sunny afternoons dry the grapes, stopping grey rot. The fungus shrivels berries and concentrates their sugar and acidity.
Mist in the morning, sun in the afternoon

Sémillon, about 80%, is the main grape, with Sauvignon Blanc and a little Muscadelle. Pickers pass through the vines several times, called tries, picking only botrytised berries. Yields are tiny. The wines ferment and age in oak, often new, reaching about 14% alcohol with 100 to 150 g/l of sugar.
Why does the Ciron river matter for Sauternes?
Its cold water creates autumn mist that favours noble rot
Mist plus afternoon sun is the recipe for noble rot.

Barsac, on flatter, limestone-based land next to Sauternes, can label its wines Barsac or Sauternes. Its wines are often slightly lighter and fresher. Climens and Coutet are famous Barsac estates. Nearby Cadillac, Loupiac and Sainte-Croix-du-Mont make lighter, cheaper sweet wines.
Barsac producers may label their wines as Sauternes.
Yes. Barsac can use either name.
The Ciron's mists bring noble rot to Sauternes
Sémillon leads; pickers make several tries
Barsac is lighter and can use either name
Reading Bordeaux and eating with it

Bordeaux labels show the château, the appellation, the vintage and often a classification, like Grand Cru Classé en 1855. Appellations run from broad to precise: Bordeaux, Bordeaux Supérieur, then district appellations like Haut-Médoc, then communes like Pauillac. Mis en bouteille au château means estate-bottled. Many châteaux also make a cheaper second wine.

Second wines, like Carruades de Lafite or Pavillon Rouge de Château Margaux, use younger vines or lots not chosen for the main wine. They offer a taste of a great estate at a lower price. Côtes de Bordeaux and Bordeaux Supérieur from good producers are often excellent value.
Second wines and Côtes for value
Order these appellations from broadest to most precise.

Left Bank reds suit lamb, especially roast leg of lamb, and steak. Right Bank Merlot suits duck, mushrooms and beef. Dry whites from Pessac-Léognan suit fish in butter sauce. Sauternes suits foie gras, Roquefort and fruit tarts. Serve reds at 16 to 18 degrees, decanted when young.
Lamb with Pauillac, foie gras with Sauternes
What does mis en bouteille au château mean?
Estate-bottled, a sign the château controlled the whole process.
Labels show château, appellation, vintage and classification
Second wines and the Côtes offer value
Lamb suits Left Bank reds; foie gras suits Sauternes
Match each place to its character.
Bordeaux's sub-regions each have a role.
Merlot is Bordeaux's most planted grape.
Saint-Émilion is on the Right Bank.
Pickers in Sauternes make several passes, called ____.
Each trie picks only the botrytised berries.
Bordeaux is maritime, built on rivers and blends
The Left Bank favours Cabernet; the Right Bank Merlot
Sauternes is its noble rot gold
